---
title: "SIS / ISIS screening for high dimensional models"
description: "Fast screening and sparse joint refitting for ultrahigh-dimensional data."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
library(L0glm)
options(width=90, digits=3)
```

**SIS** stands for **Sure Independence Screening** and **ISIS** for
**Iterative Sure Independence Screening**. These methods rapidly prescreen the
most promising predictors, after which L0glm performs joint sparse selection
and estimation. This combination gives excellent stability in high dimensional
examples and scales well to very large predictor sets. SIS was introduced by
[Fan & Lv (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00674.x), and
[Fan, Samworth & Wu (2009)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v10/fan09a.html)
developed the general likelihood-based ISIS framework. L0glm uses an offset-based
screen followed by joint sparse refitting; the controls are documented in
[`sis_glm()`](../reference/sis_glm.html).

ISIS is enabled by default for ultrahigh-dimensional models through
`screen="auto"`. Let \(n\) be the number of observations and
\(p_{\mathrm{eligible}}\) the number of eligible predictors, excluding mandatory
terms and predictors excluded by zero starts in every response channel. Automatic ISIS
is enabled when

\[
p_{\mathrm{eligible}}>10n.
\]

The same rule applies in `L0glm.tune()`, independently for each full-data or CV
training fit, using its training row count. There is no separate minimum sample
size or predictor count.

Screening keeps the full fitting interface while concentrating joint fitting
on a small, informative candidate set. Use `screen="ISIS"` to request it
explicitly at any design size.

## SIS or ISIS in one call

`screen="SIS"` performs one marginal screen. `screen="ISIS"` repeats screening
against the current model, incorporating its predictions as offsets, and keeps
the best joint-fitting round. `screen="auto"` enables ISIS for ultrahigh-dimensional
designs. `screen="none"` fits the supplied design directly.

```{r quick}
set.seed(31)
X <- matrix(rnorm(250*5000), 250, 5000)
beta <- numeric(5000); beta[c(5, 50, 500)] <- c(2, -1.5, 1)
y <- as.numeric(X %*% beta) + rnorm(250)
fit <- L0glm.fit(X, y, family=gaussian(), lambda="gic",
  screen="ISIS", screen.nthreads=2L, relaxed=TRUE)
L0glm.metrics(fit, beta_true=beta)[c("gic", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN", "F1_score", "MCC")]
```

`nsis` controls a SIS retained set or an ISIS batch. The default ISIS batch is
GIC-based. A small batch lets joint fitting remove false positives as the search
progresses. Screening is implemented in Rcpp with OpenMP and supports ordinary
GLMs, negative binomial, multinomial and Cox models.

`fit$screening` records selected predictors, screening rounds, elapsed time and
thread use. By default screening uses all physical cores, with one thread as
the fallback when detection is unavailable. Explicit `screen.nthreads` values
remain available. Coefficients always have the original dimensions, with zeros for
predictors excluded by screening.

## A million-variable example

This simulation has 500 observations, one million standard-normal predictors
and 60 nonzero effects of either sign. The dense design occupies about 4 GB.

```{r million, eval=FALSE}
n <- 500L
p <- 1000000L
set.seed(123)
X <- matrix(rnorm(n*p), n, p)
active <- sample.int(p, 60L)
beta <- numeric(p)
beta[active] <- runif(60L, -.8, .8)
set.seed(1)
y <- as.numeric(X[, active] %*% beta[active]) + rnorm(n)

fit <- L0glm.fit(X, y, family=gaussian(), lambda="gic",
  screen="ISIS", screen.nthreads=8L, nthreads=1L,
  intercept=FALSE, relaxed=TRUE)
L0glm.metrics(fit, beta_true=beta)[c("gic", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN", "F1_score", "MCC")]
```

The default L0glm fit with ISIS screening recovers **40 true effects with only
3 false positives**. It finished in just **3.49 s** using all eight physical
cores (the default). By comparison, five-fold-CV LASSO took **123.13 s**,
recovering 17 true effects with 50 false positives. The
[benchmark article](performance.html#one-million-predictor-example) reports all methods,
including relaxed LASSO, together with their tuning settings.

## Compare screening and complete models with SIS

On a Gaussian design with **500 observations and one million predictors**,
`sis_glm()` and SIS returned **identical complete screening ranks**, including
the same top 100 predictors. Screening-only median timings over three runs:

| Screening routine | Seconds |
|:--|--:|
| `sis_glm()`, eight physical cores | **0.26** |
| `sis_glm(nthreads=1)` | 0.83 |
| SIS Gaussian screen (`obtain.ix0`) | 2.16 |

The SIS row calls its screening helper directly, excluding the subsequent
LASSO fit. Gaussian correlation ranks are scale invariant, so redundant
standardization is omitted. The default OpenMP screen is about
**8.3 times faster** on this machine.

Complete screening-and-selection pipelines were timed separately. All use
BIC: L0glm uses its preset; LASSO variants search their native paths. The
one-pass comparison retains 100 predictors. On the million-predictor design,
ISIS uses the default GIC-based batch size and ten rounds. The SIS-package
ISIS comparison uses a separate 5,000-predictor design and three rounds;
`nsis=100` is a batch size in L0glm and a total support limit in SIS.
Standalone `L0glm.fit()` retains its best ISIS round by GIC; `sparseglm()`
uses the requested BIC for its outer search. Both ICs are saved with the results.

| Predictors | Screen | Complete model | Seconds | TP | FP | F1 | MCC |
|--:|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1,000,000 | SIS | SIS::SIS + BIC LASSO | 2.71 | 12 | 87 | 0.151 | 0.156 |
| 1,000,000 | SIS | L0glm.fit, BIC preset | 1.43 | 12 | 46 | 0.203 | 0.203 |
| 1,000,000 | SIS | sparseglm LASSO, BIC grid | 2.58 | 12 | 87 | 0.151 | 0.156 |
| 1,000,000 | SIS | sparseglm relaxed LASSO, BIC grid | 2.62 | 12 | 76 | 0.162 | 0.165 |
| 1,000,000 | ISIS | L0glm.fit, BIC preset | 3.52 | 7 | 12 | 0.177 | 0.207 |
| 1,000,000 | ISIS | sparseglm LASSO, BIC grid | 5.98 | 10 | 190 | 0.077 | 0.091 |
| 1,000,000 | ISIS | sparseglm relaxed LASSO, BIC grid | 6.65 | 10 | 190 | 0.077 | 0.091 |
| 5,000 | ISIS | SIS::SIS + BIC LASSO | 23.04 | 58 | 39 | 0.739 | 0.757 |
| 5,000 | ISIS | L0glm.fit, BIC preset | 0.09 | 60 | 26 | 0.822 | 0.833 |
| 5,000 | ISIS | sparseglm LASSO, BIC grid | 0.33 | 60 | 182 | 0.397 | 0.489 |
| 5,000 | ISIS | sparseglm relaxed LASSO, BIC grid | 0.39 | 60 | 57 | 0.678 | 0.712 |

`sparseglm()` also supports `screen="SIS"`, `"ISIS"`, `"auto"` and `"none"`
for every compatible method. Each ISIS search uses its own method's fitted
predictions as screening offsets. CV recomputes screening on training rows,
and returned coefficients retain every original predictor row.

```{r comparison-screening, eval=FALSE}
comparison <- sparseglm(X, y,
  method=c("L0glm", "abess", "lasso", "relaxed_lasso"),
  screen="ISIS", nsis=10, tune="gic", nlambda=10,
  lambda=list(L0glm=preset.lambda("gic", ncol(X), nrow(X))),
  options=list(L0glm=list(relaxed=TRUE)), beta_true=beta)
L0glm.metrics(comparison)[c("method", "screen", "seconds", "gic",
  "TP", "FP", "F1_score", "MCC")]
```

HP ZBook Fury G8 Mobile Workstation, Intel Core i9-11950H, eight physical cores / 16 logical cores; R 4.5.0, SIS 1.5, one BLAS thread. Timings exclude data generation. The `sparseglm` rows include
common candidate scoring and diagnostics. The [`sis_glm()` example](../reference/sis_glm.html#examples)
and [benchmark script](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/3_benchmarks_sis_vs_SIS.R)
give the calls and checks.

## GIC tuning and cross-validation

```{r tuning, eval=FALSE}
gic <- L0glm.tune(X, y, family=gaussian(), screen="ISIS",
  screen.nthreads=8L, tune="gic", nlambda=10, relaxed=TRUE)
cv <- L0glm.tune(X, y, family=gaussian(), screen="ISIS",
  screen.nthreads=8L, tune="cv", nfolds=5, nlambda=10, relaxed=TRUE)
```

Each fold screens its training observations independently. Validation can also
compare a batch grid, for example `nsis=c(2L, 5L, 10L)` with
`validation=list(X=V, y=v)`, while retaining the default GIC batch when `nsis=NULL`.
